title: Data Classification and Sensitivity Labels
monthTitle: Data Security & AI Governance with Microsoft Purview
summary: You cannot protect data you have not identified, so every Microsoft Purview data security control begins with classification. This lesson walks the full classification story: Sensitive Information Types (SITs) that pattern-match content such as credit card and national ID numbers, trainable classifiers that recognize categories like contracts by example, and sensitivity labels that carry protection such as encryption and content marking. You will build a custom employee-ID SIT from a regex with confidence and supporting evidence, then publish labels through label policies and auto-labeling policies that scan SharePoint, OneDrive, and Exchange. By the end you can design a classification taxonomy and decide where manual, recommended, and automatic labeling each belong.
objectives: Explain how Purview classification underpins DLP, Insider Risk, and Copilot data protection
Differentiate built-in versus custom Sensitive Information Types and the role of confidence and proximity
Author a custom SIT from a regex with primary and supporting evidence and a confidence level
Describe when to use trainable classifiers instead of pattern-based SITs
Configure sensitivity labels with encryption, content marking, and label scope, then publish them via a label policy
Compare manual, recommended, and automatic labeling and build an auto-labeling policy across M365 workloads

quiz.q: Why is data classification the prerequisite for almost every other Purview data security control?
options: Because classification automatically encrypts every file in the tenant
Because controls like DLP, auto-labeling, and Copilot protection act on data that has first been identified and categorized
Because classification is required to license Microsoft 365
Because it replaces the need for Conditional Access
quiz.why: DLP rules, auto-labeling, Insider Risk indicators, and Copilot exclusions all key off classified content. If the platform cannot tell that a document holds a credit card number or carries a Confidential label, no downstream policy can act on it. Classification is the foundation the rest of the stack stands on.

quiz.q: A custom Sensitive Information Type matches a 9-digit pattern but produces too many false positives on random invoice numbers. Which adjustment most directly raises precision?
options: Lower the confidence level so more matches are returned
Add supporting (corroborative) evidence such as keywords like 'Employee ID' within a proximity window and require it for a high-confidence match
Remove the regex and rely only on a trainable classifier
Publish the SIT to more locations
quiz.why: Precision improves when the primary pattern must be corroborated by supporting evidence (keywords) found within a defined character proximity. Requiring that keyword evidence for the high-confidence match suppresses bare 9-digit numbers that lack the surrounding context of a real employee ID.

quiz.q: When is a trainable classifier a better choice than a Sensitive Information Type?
options: When the data is a fixed, well-structured pattern like a 16-digit card number
When you need to recognize a category of content by its language and style, such as contracts or harassment, that has no reliable regex
When you only want to match exact dictionary terms
When you need the result instantly with no training data
quiz.why: SITs excel at structured patterns (card numbers, NHS or SSN formats). Trainable classifiers learn from sample documents to recognize fuzzy categories such as source code, contracts, or resumes that have no dependable regex. The trade-off is that a classifier must be trained and tested on examples before publishing.

quiz.q: Two sensitivity labels could both apply to a document via different auto-labeling policies. How does Purview decide which one wins?
options: The label created most recently always wins
Both labels are applied at once
Label priority (order in the list) determines precedence; the higher-priority label is applied and only one label applies at a time
The label with encryption is always skipped
quiz.why: A file carries at most one sensitivity label at a time. Labels have a priority order, and the higher-priority (typically more restrictive) label takes precedence when more than one could apply. Understanding ordering is essential when designing overlapping auto-labeling policies.

quiz.q: What is the practical effect of a sensitivity label that applies encryption with a 'Co-Author' permission set scoped to your finance team?
options: Anyone with the file link can open and edit it
The protection travels with the file, and only the assigned finance users get the granted rights even if the file leaves the tenant
The file is deleted after 30 days
Only content marking (a footer) is added with no access control
quiz.why: Label-applied encryption uses Azure Rights Management, so the usage rights are bound to the content itself. Wherever the file travels, only the assigned identities receive the granted rights (such as co-author), which is why labels protect data even outside the tenant boundary.

quiz.q: Your organization wants users to label most documents themselves but wants Purview to suggest a label when a file clearly contains regulated data, without forcing it. In two to four sentences, explain how manual, recommended, and automatic labeling differ and which combination fits this requirement.
quiz.answer: Manual labeling lets users pick a label from the bar themselves, recommended labeling shows a policy tip suggesting a specific label when matching content is detected but leaves the final choice to the user, and automatic labeling applies a label with no user interaction based on conditions. The requirement is best met by enabling manual labeling as the default and adding a recommended-labeling condition (for example, when a financial or PII SIT is detected) so users are prompted but retain control. You can later add service-side auto-labeling policies for high-confidence cases where user discretion is not needed.
quiz.why: The scenario explicitly wants user discretion preserved while nudging correct behavior, which is exactly the recommended-labeling pattern layered on top of manual labeling, with automatic labeling reserved for cases that should not depend on a user's choice.

resources.label: Create a custom sensitive information type

body_markdown:
## Classification Is the Foundation

Every data protection control you will build in this module, DLP rules, Insider Risk indicators, and Copilot guardrails, depends on one thing: the platform knowing **what** a piece of content is. Microsoft Purview answers that question through **data classification**. If Purview can recognize that a spreadsheet holds credit card numbers, or that a document carries a `Confidential` label, then downstream policies can encrypt it, block its sharing, or hide it from Copilot. If it cannot, nothing else can act. So we start here.

Classification in Purview has three engines that work together:

- **Sensitive Information Types (SITs)** - pattern matchers for structured data.
- **Trainable classifiers** - machine-learned recognizers for fuzzy categories.
- **Sensitivity labels** - the durable tags that carry protection and travel with the data.

## Sensitive Information Types: Built-in and Custom

A **SIT** detects a specific kind of content, usually by a regular expression plus corroborating evidence. Microsoft ships hundreds of **built-in SITs**: U.S. Social Security Number, credit card number (validated with the Luhn checksum), IBAN, passport and national ID numbers for dozens of countries, and more. You can use these immediately in DLP and auto-labeling.

When your data is organization-specific, you build a **custom SIT**. A SIT match is more than a regex; it is tuned with:

- **Primary element** - the core pattern (the regex or a keyword list).
- **Supporting / corroborative evidence** - additional keywords or patterns that must appear nearby.
- **Proximity** - how many characters apart the primary and supporting evidence may be (default 300).
- **Confidence level** - low, medium, or high, reflecting how much corroboration was required.

More corroboration means higher precision (fewer false positives) at the cost of recall. You typically reference the **high confidence** match in production policies.

## Worked Example: A Custom Employee-ID SIT

Suppose every employee ID at Contoso looks like `EMP-` followed by 6 digits, e.g. `EMP-004217`. A bare regex would also fire on unrelated strings, so we add supporting keywords.

```text
Primary pattern (regex):   EMP-\d{6}
Supporting keywords:       "employee id", "emp id", "staff number", "personnel"
Proximity:                 300 characters
Confidence:                High = regex match AND a supporting keyword within proximity
                           Medium = regex match alone
```

In the Purview portal you go to **Data classification > Classifiers > Sensitive info types > Create**, define the **primary element** with the regex, add a **supporting elements** group containing the keyword list, set the **character proximity**, and assign the **confidence level** for each combination. Always use **Test** with sample text before publishing: paste a few real-looking and decoy strings and confirm the high-confidence rule only fires when a keyword is present.

## Trainable Classifiers

Some content has no reliable pattern. There is no regex for "this is a legal contract" or "this is source code" or "this looks like harassment." For these, Purview offers **trainable classifiers**. Microsoft provides many **pre-trained** classifiers (Resumes, Source Code, Contracts, Threat, Profanity, and more) that are ready to use. For organization-specific categories you create a **custom trainable classifier**: you feed it 50+ positive sample documents, let it learn, then **test** it against a separate set and review its accuracy before publishing. Use a classifier when you are categorizing by meaning and style rather than by a fixed format; use a SIT when the data is structured.

## Sensitivity Labels and Label Policies

A **sensitivity label** is a persistent, human-readable tag, for example `Public`, `General`, `Confidential`, `Highly Confidential`, that can also enforce protection. A label can:

- **Encrypt** content (via Azure Rights Management), binding usage rights such as view or co-author to specific users or groups, so protection travels with the file even outside the tenant.
- **Apply content marking** - headers, footers, and watermarks (e.g. a `CONFIDENTIAL` footer).
- **Control container, meeting, and site settings**, and govern access for groups and SharePoint sites.

Labels are organized in a priority-ordered list and may have **sublabels**. A file carries **one label at a time**; when more than one could apply, the **higher-priority** label wins. Labels also have a **scope** (items, groups and sites, schematized data assets), which decides where they can be used.

Labels do nothing until **published**. A **label policy** publishes a chosen set of labels to specific users and groups and configures behavior such as a **default label**, whether a **justification** is required to lower a label, and whether labeling is **mandatory**.

## Manual, Recommended, and Automatic Labeling

There are three ways a label gets applied:

- **Manual** - the user selects a label from the Sensitivity bar in Office apps. Maximum user control, depends on user diligence.
- **Recommended** - when a label policy detects matching content (e.g. a financial SIT), the app shows a **policy tip** suggesting a label, but the user decides. A good balance of guidance and control.
- **Automatic** - the label is applied with no user interaction. This happens **client-side** (in Office apps as the user works) or **service-side** via an **auto-labeling policy**.

## Auto-Labeling Policies Across M365

**Auto-labeling policies** run in the service and scan content at rest and in transit across **SharePoint, OneDrive, and Exchange**. You define **conditions** (which SITs or trainable classifiers, at what confidence, and a minimum instance count) and the **label** to apply. Best practice is to run the policy in **simulation mode** first: Purview reports which items *would* be labeled so you can validate accuracy and tune conditions before turning enforcement on. Once confident, you enable the policy and it labels existing and new matching content. Combined with client-side automatic labeling, this gives you coverage for both data being created and the large back catalog of data already sitting in your tenant, which is exactly the readiness work that later makes DLP and Copilot protection effective.

slides.sub: The Purview foundation every other control depends on
slides.narration: Welcome to Module 3 on data security and AI governance with Microsoft Purview. Before we can prevent data loss, detect insider risk, or make Microsoft 365 Copilot safe, we have to teach the platform what our data actually is. This lesson is the foundation: sensitive information types, trainable classifiers, and sensitivity labels. Get classification right and everything downstream becomes possible.

slides.title: Why Classification Comes First
bullets: DLP, Insider Risk, and Copilot controls all act on classified data
If Purview cannot identify content, no policy can protect it
Three engines: SITs, trainable classifiers, sensitivity labels
Classification is the base layer of the whole module
slides.narration: Every control we build later keys off classification. A DLP rule that blocks credit card numbers, a Copilot exclusion for confidential files, an Insider Risk indicator for sensitive downloads, none of them work unless Purview first recognizes the data. Purview classifies using three cooperating engines: sensitive information types for patterns, trainable classifiers for fuzzy categories, and sensitivity labels that carry protection.

slides.title: Sensitive Information Types
bullets: Pattern matchers for structured data like card and ID numbers
Hundreds of built-in SITs, validated (e.g. Luhn for cards)
Tuned with primary pattern, supporting evidence, proximity
Confidence level trades recall for precision
slides.narration: A sensitive information type detects a specific kind of content. Microsoft ships hundreds of built-in SITs for things like social security numbers and credit cards, many with checksum validation. A SIT is more than a regex: it combines a primary pattern with supporting keyword evidence found within a proximity window, and assigns a confidence level. The more corroboration you require, the higher the precision.

slides.title: Worked Example: Custom Employee-ID SIT
bullets: Pattern: EMP- followed by six digits
Add supporting keywords to suppress false positives
High confidence requires regex AND a nearby keyword
Always Test with real and decoy samples before publishing
slides.code:
Primary regex:      EMP-\d{6}
Supporting words:   "employee id", "staff number"
Proximity:          300 characters
High confidence:    regex + keyword within proximity
Medium confidence:  regex alone
slides.narration: Here is a concrete custom SIT. Contoso employee IDs are EMP dash six digits. A bare regex would also match random strings, so we add supporting keywords like employee id within a three hundred character proximity, and we only treat it as high confidence when both the pattern and a keyword appear. Before publishing, we use the Test pane with real-looking and decoy text to confirm it fires only when it should.

slides.title: Trainable Classifiers
bullets: For categories with no reliable regex: contracts, source code, resumes
Pre-trained classifiers ready to use out of the box
Custom classifiers learn from 50+ sample documents
Test against a separate set and review accuracy before publishing
slides.narration: Some content cannot be matched by a pattern. There is no regex for this is a contract or this is harassment. Trainable classifiers learn these fuzzy categories from examples. Purview ships several pre-trained classifiers, and you can build custom ones by supplying at least fifty positive samples, then testing accuracy on a separate set. Use a classifier for meaning and style, a SIT for structured formats.

slides.title: Sensitivity Labels Carry Protection
bullets: Persistent tags: Public, General, Confidential, Highly Confidential
Can encrypt via Azure Rights Management and bind usage rights
Can add content marking: headers, footers, watermarks
Protection travels with the file, even outside the tenant
slides.narration: A sensitivity label is a durable tag that can also enforce protection. A label can encrypt content with Azure Rights Management, binding rights like view or co-author to named users so only they can open it, even if the file leaves your tenant. Labels can also stamp visual markings like a confidential footer. This is what makes a label more than metadata: the protection sticks to the data itself.

slides.title: Labels, Priority, and Label Policies
bullets: A file carries one label at a time
Priority order decides which label wins when several could apply
Labels do nothing until published by a label policy
Policies set default label, mandatory labeling, and justification
slides.narration: Labels live in a priority-ordered list and can have sublabels, but a file only ever carries one label at a time. When more than one could apply, the higher-priority, usually more restrictive, label wins. Labels do nothing until a label policy publishes them to users. That policy also configures a default label, whether labeling is mandatory, and whether users must justify lowering a label.

slides.title: Manual, Recommended, Automatic Labeling
bullets: Manual: user picks from the Sensitivity bar
Recommended: policy tip suggests a label, user decides
Automatic: applied with no user interaction
Automatic runs client-side in apps or service-side in policies
slides.narration: Labels get applied in three ways. Manual gives the user full control. Recommended shows a policy tip nudging the user toward a label when matching content is found, but leaves the decision to them. Automatic applies the label with no interaction, either client-side as the user works in Office, or service-side through an auto-labeling policy. Most organizations blend all three.

slides.title: Auto-Labeling Across M365
bullets: Service-side policies scan SharePoint, OneDrive, and Exchange
Conditions: which SITs or classifiers, confidence, instance count
Run in simulation mode first to validate accuracy
Labels existing back catalog plus new content
slides.narration: Auto-labeling policies run in the service and scan data at rest and in transit across SharePoint, OneDrive, and Exchange. You set conditions on SITs or classifiers and the label to apply. Always start in simulation mode, which reports what would be labeled so you can tune before enforcing. This is how you label the huge back catalog of existing data, the readiness work that makes DLP and Copilot protection effective later in this module.
